paragraphs: AnyCanvas addresses image generation inside irregular boundaries. A text-to-image system may produce an appealing picture while failing to fit the shape required for packaging or a logo. The challenge is to satisfy that spatial constraint without losing the meaning of the requested image or producing an incomplete composition.

The framework translates a binary mask, which specifies the allowed region, into a differentiable potential field. This gives the generation process a spatial signal that can guide content toward the target area. The approach requires no additional training. Its central contribution is therefore a way to express arbitrary canvas shapes as guidance that an existing diffusion model can use during generation.

The experiments report 4.23% higher spatial adherence while retaining 99.45% of semantic fidelity as measured by CLIP score. Their combined spatial-and-semantic measure also improves. These findings support the usefulness of balancing shape compliance with preservation of prompt meaning. The authors additionally report generalization across different model backbones and multiple spatial-control objectives.
icml-2026-anycanvas-potential-field-guid.tldr: AnyCanvas guides diffusion models to fit arbitrary canvas shapes without additional training while largely preserving prompt meaning.

paragraphs: APE-Bench addresses the gap between proving an isolated theorem and modifying a formal mathematics library. Repository work can require coordinated changes across several files, and a result that compiles may still fail to satisfy the requested mathematical or engineering requirements. The paper makes those broader obligations part of evaluation.

The proposed Automated Proof Engineering framework checks two things: whether the artifact compiles and whether it fulfills its semantic requirements. Evaluations use fixed library environments so that agents face consistent conditions. APE-Bench extracts tasks automatically from actual library commit histories, while APE-Harness provides a common execution framework organized around explicit task contracts.

Those contracts allow different agent implementations to be compared on identical specifications. The evaluation includes the authors’ APE-Agent scaffold alongside Claude Code and Codex CLI. The authors report that their evaluation demonstrates the framework’s effectiveness. The contribution is an infrastructure for assessing repository-scale proof engineering, with both executable validity and requirement satisfaction represented in the assessment.
icml-2026-ape-bench-evaluating-automated.tldr: APE-Bench evaluates formal mathematics agents on repository tasks using both compilation checks and semantic requirement checks.

paragraphs: AREA studies how a CLIP-based classifier can learn new classes without forgetting earlier ones. It separates image–text matching into recognizing attributes and combining those attributes into a class representation. Learning a car, for example, requires identifying wheels and integrating them into the shared representation. When only current-task data is available, both processes can shift toward new classes.

To stabilize attribute extraction, AREA anchors class-level visual and textual attributes in the model’s spherical embedding space using principal geodesic analysis. To stabilize their combination, it learns small task-specific experts that score and refine representations. An information-bottleneck objective regularizes these experts, making the organization of attributes an explicit part of incremental learning.

At prediction time, optimal transport routes inputs across the attribute structures associated with different tasks. The design addresses forgetting at several stages rather than treating image–text similarity as one indivisible operation. Experiments report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, supporting this separation of attribute extraction, aggregation, and inference routing for the evaluated class-incremental settings.
icml-2026-area-attribute-extraction-and-.tldr: AREA reduces forgetting in CLIP-based incremental learning by stabilizing how attributes are extracted, combined, and routed.

paragraphs: Split federated learning divides a model between participating clients and a server. When clients hold differently distributed data, their contributions can bias the shared training process and make convergence unstable. BESplit starts from the observation that this split also creates opportunities to coordinate information through intermediate representations, beyond simply combining model parameters.

The framework uses three complementary mechanisms. Evidential Aggregation reweights client contributions using uncertainty derived from evidence, aiming to prevent biased local data from dominating updates. Bias-Compensated Collaboration pairs complementary clients and aligns their representations at the split layer. Dual-Teacher Distillation then synchronizes knowledge between the separated client and server models, supporting inference locally without requiring the server.

Together, these mechanisms address contribution weighting, representation mismatch, and knowledge synchronization. Experiments on five benchmark datasets report consistently better accuracy, convergence stability, and computational efficiency than state-of-the-art methods across diverse non-IID settings. The findings support treating the split architecture itself as a resource for handling client differences, rather than relying only on adaptations of conventional federated-learning aggregation.
icml-2026-besplit-bias-compensated-split.tldr: BESplit uses uncertainty weighting, complementary client pairing, and distillation to improve split federated learning with uneven client data.

paragraphs: BFS-Prover-V2 tackles two ways to improve automated theorem proving: train a stronger model for individual proof steps, and organize more effective search when solving a theorem. The paper treats these as complementary scaling problems, since better training and more inference-time computation each need mechanisms that make continued investment useful.

For training, it introduces multi-turn off-policy reinforcement learning with repeated expert iteration. Adaptive filtering selects tactic-level training data, and periodic retraining aims to overcome performance plateaus. For inference, a general reasoning model plans by repeatedly decomposing a difficult theorem into simpler subgoals. Parallel prover agents work on the resulting search while sharing a proof cache, helping coordinate their efforts.

The authors report state-of-the-art benchmark results, including 95.08% on miniF2F and 41.4% on ProofNet test sets. These results support combining stronger step-level learning with hierarchical, collaborative search. The paper also suggests that the techniques may transfer to other long-horizon reasoning and search problems, but the reported demonstration is in formal mathematics.
icml-2026-bfs-prover-v2-scaling-up-multi.tldr: BFS-Prover-V2 combines iterative reinforcement learning with planner-guided parallel proof search to improve formal theorem proving.

paragraphs: A pass-or-fail score for a proof hint reveals little about whether a language model can reconstruct the deductions needed to verify Rust code. This paper addresses that evaluation gap by making the intermediate verification process explicit. Its focus is the ability to supply the reasoning steps underlying verification, beyond obtaining a successful final outcome.

VCoT-Lift converts low-level solver reasoning into readable verification steps. Those steps provide a reference for VCoT-Bench, which contains 1,988 completion tasks. The benchmark varies how much proof material is missing, the type of proof involved, and the location of the missing material. These three dimensions expose different ways a model’s reconstruction can succeed or fail.

Evaluation of ten state-of-the-art models finds severe fragility. The reported results indicate that these models fall well short of automated theorem provers on the verification reasoning being tested. By showing where reconstruction breaks down, the benchmark offers a more detailed assessment of Rust verification ability than a single binary score for submitted hints.
icml-2026-can-llms-reason-like-automated.tldr: VCoT-Bench exposes substantial weaknesses in LLM Rust verification by testing reconstruction of explicit solver-derived proof steps.

paragraphs: DPsurv addresses survival prediction from whole-slide pathology images. These images contain information at both cellular and tissue scales, but their heterogeneous content makes it important to explain predictions and represent uncertainty. The paper targets existing methods that provide limited interpretability or overlook uncertainty when turning slide features into survival estimates.

Its dual-prototype network produces survival intervals that account for predictive uncertainty. The explanation process follows three stages: assigning image patches to prototype distributions, reasoning about evidence through component prototypes, and aggregating relative risk across components. This gives the prediction a structured path from local image features through intermediate evidence to the final risk assessment.

Experiments on five public datasets report strong discrimination and well-calibrated predictions. Discrimination concerns separating different survival outcomes, while calibration concerns how well predictions align with observed outcomes. The authors also describe transparency at the feature, reasoning, and decision levels. Together, these findings support the proposed combination of uncertainty-aware output and a traceable explanation of how slide information contributes to survival predictions.
icml-2026-dpsurv-dual-prototype-evidenti.tldr: DPsurv combines prototype-based evidence and risk aggregation to produce interpretable, uncertainty-aware survival predictions from pathology slides.

paragraphs: This paper studies online learning when the best decision can change over time. Dynamic regret measures performance against that changing comparison point. The focus is follow-the-regularized-leader methods, whose dynamic-regret analysis is less developed despite their relevance to curved losses and to understanding adaptive optimizers such as Adam.

The authors build a modular analysis around a discounted-to-dynamic reduction. The reduction connects analysis that discounts past information with guarantees against a changing comparator. For online linear regression, it simplifies existing proofs of optimal dynamic regret. For online logistic regression, it supplies new dynamic-regret guarantees. A shared analytical tool therefore supports results for two distinct curved-loss problems.

The paper also applies this reduction to Adam, obtaining optimal convergence rates in the stochastic, non-convex, and non-smooth settings it analyzes. It explicitly treats Adam’s two discount parameters, producing new results for variants with and without clipping. The contribution is theoretical: a reusable route to regret and convergence guarantees across several related optimization problems.
icml-2026-dynamic-regret-via-discounted-.tldr: A modular discounted-to-dynamic reduction yields regret guarantees for online regression and convergence results for Adam variants.

paragraphs: FedVeer addresses federated learning with uneven client data distributions. Some existing methods estimate a client’s data skew from the density of neighboring model updates. The paper identifies two problems with that approach: fixed neighborhoods can favor a skewed majority, and noisy updates can disturb the estimates in the kernel representation used for density estimation.

The proposed framework chooses neighborhood sizes adaptively instead of requiring a fixed number of neighbors. It uses max-margin learning to determine these neighborhoods and reduce majority-client bias. Kalman filtering stabilizes margin estimation when updates are noisy. The authors also provide a high-probability theoretical bound on margin deviation, connecting the stabilization mechanism to a formal guarantee.

Experiments on real-world datasets report consistent improvements over four baselines. The largest reported accuracy improvement is 6.36%, and the largest reduction in noise-induced degradation is 6.01%. These are best reported gains across the experiments. The results support adapting both the neighborhood structure and its noise handling when estimating skew from client updates.
icml-2026-fedveer-self-adaptive-skew-est.tldr: FedVeer estimates client skew with adaptive neighborhoods and filtered margins to improve federated learning under uneven and noisy updates.

paragraphs: FG-CLIP 2 targets image–text matching that depends on small but meaningful details: object attributes, spatial relationships, and precise wording. Broad agreement between an image and a caption does not necessarily capture those distinctions. The paper also addresses limited bilingual support by developing fine-grained alignment for both English and Chinese.

Training combines region–text matching, long-caption modeling, and multiple discriminative objectives. A textual contrastive loss helps separate captions that are semantically similar but still meaningfully different. The training mixture includes large-scale English and Chinese data, with a newly released Chinese region–text dataset containing 12 million examples. These ingredients bring supervision to both visual detail and linguistic distinctions.

The authors introduce a Chinese multimodal benchmark covering long-caption retrieval and bounding-box classification. Across 29 datasets and eight tasks, they report improvements over existing methods and state-of-the-art results in both languages. The findings support the value of detailed supervision and caption discrimination for bilingual alignment, while the released model, code, and benchmark provide resources for further study.
icml-2026-fg-clip-2-a-bilingual-fine-gra.tldr: FG-CLIP 2 improves detailed English–Chinese image–text alignment through region supervision, long captions, and contrastive caption discrimination.

paragraphs: GePBench examines whether multimodal language models can recognize geometric shapes and understand their spatial relationships. The paper calls this combination geometric perception. Although these models have made progress in general visual understanding, that progress leaves a separate question: how reliably can they perceive the basic geometric structure of what they see?

The authors create a benchmark specifically for that question and evaluate current models on it. Their extensive evaluation finds substantial deficiencies even among state-of-the-art systems. The benchmark makes geometric perception an explicit evaluation target, allowing weaknesses in shapes and spatial relationships to be studied as capabilities in their own right.

The paper also investigates whether training on GePBench data helps beyond the benchmark itself. It reports considerable improvements across a wide range of downstream tasks after such training. That finding suggests geometric perception can support broader multimodal abilities, rather than being useful only for answering geometry questions. The contribution combines a diagnostic evaluation resource with evidence that strengthening the tested capability can benefit other tasks.
icml-2026-gepbench-evaluating-fundamenta.tldr: GePBench reveals weaknesses in multimodal models’ geometric perception and shows that training on its data improves downstream performance.

paragraphs: IDEAL-VLN addresses navigation guided by long, complex instructions. Continuously conditioning actions on the entire instruction can introduce irrelevant text into each decision, contributing to hallucinations. Processing abundant visual tokens also adds latency. The paper reorganizes navigation so that the system first identifies the immediate meaning relevant to its next action.

Its two stages are Semantic Anchoring and Action Alignment. The first derives an immediate semantic anchor from the global context; the second generates actions conditioned only on that anchor. This creates an explicit information bottleneck intended to suppress irrelevant instruction correlations. During training, a hierarchical correction scheme combines corrections to semantic reasoning with expert intervention whose probability changes according to geodesic distance.

The authors contribute an instruction-aligned dataset of 160,000 image–text pairs to support this approach. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance and robustness across major benchmarks, alongside significantly reduced inference costs. The findings support separating interpretation of the current navigation objective from action generation, with training corrections helping address cognitive collapse and limited exploration.
icml-2026-instruction-decomposition-and-.tldr: IDEAL-VLN extracts an immediate instruction anchor before acting, improving navigation performance while reducing inference costs.

paragraphs: This paper studies video hallucinations caused by incorrectly combining several spatial and temporal factors. Such errors go beyond a single mistaken detail. The authors introduce OmniVCHall to evaluate both isolated and compositional hallucinations across diverse video domains, including a new category involving cameras and a detailed taxonomy of errors.

The benchmark includes adversarial answer choices such as options asserting that every answer, or no answer, is correct. These are designed to discourage shortcut reasoning. Evaluations of 39 video language models reveal substantial degradation even in advanced systems. The results motivate TriCD, a contrastive decoding framework that calibrates generation through three pathways.

TriCD adaptively creates distracting video variants and strengthens visual evidence relevant to individual output tokens using saliency guidance. Reinforcement learning optimizes these components for decisions involving compositional hallucinations. Across two representative backbones, the method consistently improves performance, with average accuracy gains above 10%. The findings support combining challenging evaluation with decoding mechanisms that explicitly distinguish distracting inputs from grounded visual evidence.
icml-2026-learning-to-decode-against-com.tldr: OmniVCHall tests interacting video hallucinations, while TriCD improves decoding by contrasting distractions with reinforced visual evidence.

paragraphs: MEMO addresses both weak performance and unstable evaluation in multi-agent language-model games. Small differences can accumulate across turns and spread through interactions between agents, producing variable win rates and rankings. Prompt choices add another source of variation because they change how agents behave throughout a game.

The framework optimizes the context used at inference through self-play. Its retention component condenses gameplay trajectories into persistent, structured insights that guide later decisions. Its exploration component evolves prompts through tournaments using TrueSkill and prioritizes replay of decisive states. This combines keeping useful experience with searching for better strategies expressed through context.

Across five text-based games with 2,000 games per task, mean win rates rise from 25.1% to 49.5% for GPT-4o-mini and from 20.9% to 45.0% for Qwen-2.5-7B. Run-to-run dispersion also falls sharply. The gains include negotiation and imperfect-information settings; reinforcement learning remains more effective in perfect-information settings. The results suggest substantial scope for improving game performance and consistency through memory and context optimization.
icml-2026-memo-memory-augmented-model-co.tldr: MEMO combines persistent self-play memory and prompt evolution to raise game win rates and reduce run-to-run variability.

paragraphs: Hyper-Connections expand residual streams and introduce more varied connections within a neural network. The paper explains that this flexibility can improve performance but disrupts the identity-mapping property of ordinary residual connections—the ability to preserve information unchanged along the residual path. That disruption is associated with severe training instability and limited scalability, alongside additional memory-access costs.

Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections restrict the allowable residual connections to a particular structured space. The framework projects the connection space onto this manifold to restore the identity-mapping property. It also includes infrastructure optimization to address efficiency, treating the mathematical connection design and its implementation costs as parts of the same scaling problem.

Experiments report effective large-scale training, performance improvements, and better scalability. These results support constraining expanded connectivity so that it retains a useful property of residual networks. The authors present mHC as a flexible extension of Hyper-Connections and suggest it could inform future architectural research; that broader influence is an anticipated direction rather than an experimental finding.
icml-2026-mhc-manifold-constrained-hyper.tldr: mHC constrains Hyper-Connections to restore identity mapping, improving large-scale training stability, performance, and scalability.

paragraphs: OmniAgent approaches long-video understanding as an active search for relevant evidence. Uniformly processing frames makes computation grow with video length, and interactive systems can retain that dependence when they first scan the whole video. OmniAgent instead uses repeated observation, thought, and action to decide what audio-visual information to inspect on demand.

The agent summarizes selected cues into persistent textual memory. Its decision process uses a partially observable formulation, allowing reasoning to proceed from accumulated evidence. Training begins with supervised learning from selected synthetic trajectories under two stages of quality control. Reinforcement learning then uses TAURA, which draws on turn-level entropy to assign credit toward pivotal evidence-discovery turns.

The authors report that performance improves as the agent receives more reasoning turns. Across ten benchmarks, it achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models. On LVBench, its 7B model scores 50.5%, compared with 47.3% for Qwen2.5-VL-72B. These findings support selective perception and persistent memory as an effective way to allocate reasoning effort in long-video understanding.
icml-2026-native-active-perception-as-re.tldr: OmniAgent learns to inspect video evidence on demand and retain textual memory, with performance improving through additional reasoning turns.

paragraphs: PretrainZero aims to broaden reasoning training beyond domains with readily verifiable rewards. Reinforcement learning has produced strong mathematical and software abilities, but dependence on specialized verification data can restrict expansion to general reasoning. The paper uses ordinary pretraining text as the material for an active reinforcement-learning process.

A unified reasoning policy learns to identify reasonable, informative content in the corpus and reason toward predicting it. Training tackles increasingly challenging masked spans. The authors apply this process to base models ranging from 3B to 30B parameters on Wikipedia, without verifiable labels, pretrained reward models, or supervised fine-tuning. Content selection and prediction are therefore combined within the proposed learning framework.

For Qwen3-4B-Base, the reported benchmark gains are 8.43 on MMLU-Pro, 5.96 on SuperGPQA, and 10.60 on the math average. The authors also state that the resulting models can provide a reasoning foundation for downstream reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. The findings support using pretraining corpora to extend the range of material available for reasoning-oriented reinforcement learning.
icml-2026-pretrainzero-reinforcement-act.tldr: PretrainZero trains reasoning through reinforcement learning that selects and predicts informative masked content in general pretraining text.

paragraphs: This paper investigates which training data can strengthen reasoning over long contexts and why it helps. Its focus is structured tables with recurring organization. The authors identify periodic dependencies that remain present across table data, suggesting that these structures can provide useful material for learning to connect information across a long input.

They analyze those dependencies mathematically through mutual information and study the capabilities and scaling behavior of table-based data. Building on the resulting insights, they introduce TableLong, a pipeline for generating diverse, verifiable structured tables at scale. The generated data is used in reinforcement learning to improve long-context reasoning.

Experiments report an average improvement of 8.24% across multiple long-context benchmarks and 8.06% on out-of-domain benchmarks. The latter result indicates that the observed gains extend beyond the immediate training domain in the evaluations. The contribution combines an explanation of a useful data property with a practical synthesis pipeline, providing evidence that structured tables can support broader long-context abilities.
icml-2026-probing-how-scalable-table-dat.tldr: TableLong uses scalable, verifiable table data for reinforcement learning, improving long-context reasoning and out-of-domain benchmark performance.

paragraphs: pTNAS searches for neural-network architectures suited to tabular datasets under a limited computation budget. The paper motivates this with the inference costs of tabular foundation models and the competitiveness of well-designed conventional networks. Its goal is to find a viable architecture quickly, then improve the search result as more resources become available.

The search first filters a large architecture space using pTProxy, an evaluation signal that requires no network training. This proxy considers both trainability and expressivity. A second stage trains and evaluates a small set of promising candidates using a fixed-budget schedule. A budget-aware coordinator allocates resources across the overall process, linking cheap screening with more accurate refinement.

Experiments report up to an 82.75-fold reduction in time to reach the globally best architecture compared with other architecture-search approaches. pTNAS also obtains the best average predictive rank and up to a 4.78-fold improvement in end-to-end efficiency compared with TabPFN. These results support progressive search as a way to make tabular network design responsive to available resources.
icml-2026-ptnas-progressive-neural-archi.tldr: pTNAS combines training-free filtering and budgeted refinement to find effective tabular network architectures efficiently.

paragraphs: CSteer addresses a gap between understanding an image as a whole and interpreting specific visually indicated regions. The problem becomes harder when several regions are referenced together or when understanding a region requires broader image context. General multimodal models can struggle with those demands despite strong holistic visual comprehension.

The method precomputes contextual vectors that implicitly encode useful referring behaviors. These include distinguishing between regions and attending to global context. During inference, it edits the model’s internal representations using those vectors. This steers an existing general model toward contextual region-level behavior without fine-tuning or changes to its architecture.

Across multiple datasets, the authors report that general multimodal models equipped with CSteer outperform specialized referring models in most cases and achieve new state-of-the-art results. The qualification matters: the reported advantage is not universal across every evaluated case. The findings suggest that representation editing can make existing visual abilities more useful for simultaneous, context-sensitive region references without requiring a separately trained referring model.
icml-2026-referring-multiple-regions-wit.tldr: CSteer edits internal representations at inference to improve contextual understanding of multiple image regions without additional training.

paragraphs: SAME studies multimodal instruction tuning as new tasks arrive over time. Sparse expert models can specialize, but continual learning creates two distinct failures. The router may stop choosing the experts previously used for a task, and the experts themselves may lose earlier functionality as new tasks change their parameters.

To stabilize routing, SAME separates routing changes into orthogonal subspaces and updates only directions relevant to the current task. To protect experts, it scales updates using curvature information derived from historical input covariance, without rehearsing old examples. Adaptive expert activation also freezes selected experts during training to reduce unnecessary computation and interference across tasks.

These components address both access to previously useful expertise and preservation of that expertise. The authors introduce a benchmark with long task sequences and report state-of-the-art performance in extensive experiments. The results support treating router drift and expert drift as separate continual-learning problems that require coordinated controls, rather than assuming task specialization alone will preserve earlier multimodal capabilities.
icml-2026-same-stabilized-mixture-of-exp.tldr: SAME stabilizes expert selection and expert updates to preserve multimodal capabilities during continual instruction tuning.

paragraphs: SkillNet addresses transfer to unfamiliar behaviors and new combinations of tasks in vision-language action models. Its starting point is that repeatable, atomic skills share useful attributes. Existing skill-based approaches can leave those relationships loosely organized and lack a structured parameter representation through which shared attributes influence transfer.

The method organizes skills hierarchically using motion codes and the VerbNet framework. These capture similarities in mechanical properties and semantic roles. It then uses skill embeddings as soft constraints within a mixture-of-experts model, encouraging similar skills to activate similar experts. The hierarchy therefore shapes how the model shares computation across behaviors while retaining differences between skills.

Experiments include zero-shot and few-shot transfer in simulated and real-world environments, with reported performance improvements of 16.0% and 23.9%, respectively. SkillNet also reaches state-of-the-art performance in the in-domain settings. The findings support connecting an explicit organization of skill relationships to expert activation as a route toward learning behaviors that can be recombined and transferred.
icml-2026-skillnet-hierarchical-skill-mo.tldr: SkillNet organizes skills hierarchically and guides expert activation with shared attributes to improve compositional action transfer.

paragraphs: Reasoning models sometimes continue generating unnecessary steps, especially when a query is ambiguous or poorly posed. This paper asks whether uncertainty signals during generation can guide a principled stopping decision. The objective is to reduce unproductive reasoning while accounting for the risk of stopping too soon on a question that can be answered.

The authors introduce two statistical approaches. The nonparametric method provides finite-sample guarantees on the probability of premature stopping for well-posed queries. The parametric method models the gaps between uncertainty-related keywords as a renewal process, then uses sequential testing to decide when to stop. The two methods provide different routes from observed uncertainty to a stopping rule.

Evaluations across several reasoning domains and models indicate that uncertainty-aware stopping can improve efficiency and reliability together. The effects vary by domain, with particularly strong gains in mathematics. The theoretical guarantee is specifically about premature halting on well-posed queries; the broader usefulness of the methods is supported by the reported empirical evaluations.
icml-2026-statistical-early-stopping-for.tldr: Statistical stopping rules use uncertainty during generation to reduce excessive reasoning, with especially strong reported gains in mathematics.

paragraphs: TEP-SAM addresses small targets that are difficult to distinguish from background noise in infrared video. A single frame may contain too little visible evidence for reliable detection, even when a strong segmentation model is available. The paper instead draws on the observation that a target can become distinguishable as its behavior unfolds over time.

The framework jointly models broad motion patterns and local departures from those patterns to locate possible targets. It then uses motion discrepancies to strengthen features in candidate target regions. The resulting temporal cues modulate and prompt the Segment Anything Model, allowing segmentation without interactive prompting by a person.

This links SAM’s large-scale semantic pretraining with motion information specific to infrared target detection. Experiments report effectiveness especially under very low signal-to-noise conditions and complex, changing backgrounds. The findings support explicitly constructing cues from how targets emerge over time, rather than expecting individual frames or general inter-frame association alone to provide sufficiently clear evidence for segmentation.
icml-2026-temporal-emerged-prompting-for.tldr: TEP-SAM turns temporal motion differences into automatic prompts for segmenting faint, small infrared targets.

paragraphs: This paper builds a multimodal assistant by coordinating existing modality experts. Jointly training an integrated system can demand substantial data and computation and complicate later extensions. The proposed orchestration framework combines off-the-shelf components without additional gradient-based training for their integration, making coordination the central design problem.

An LLM controller interprets user intent and emits explicit control tokens to select and sequence experts. This makes routing constrained by a protocol and available for inspection. A text-centered memory compresses multimodal evidence into structured records that can be retrieved across turns, reducing repeated expert calls. A unified interaction layer executes these decisions and handles modality transitions, simultaneous two-way streaming, and interruptions.

Across diverse multimodal benchmarks, the framework reports strong performance under standard evaluation constraints with low orchestration overhead. Its modular design also supports upgrading components. These findings present orchestration as a practical alternative to costly joint training for the evaluated systems, with memory and interaction management contributing alongside the controller’s choice of experts.
icml-2026-training-free-multimodal-large.tldr: An LLM controller, structured memory, and interaction layer combine existing modality experts without additional integration training.
